content: Surveys conducted in Lesotho (2019), Myanmar (2018), and South Africa (2017–2019), along with two subnational surveys in South Africa and Zambia as part of the TREATS study (2019), classified trace calls as positive based on results from a single Xpert Ultra test. The culture methods used varied: Myanmar employed Ogawa solid culture, while other countries utilized liquid culture (MGIT). The diagnostic performance of Xpert Ultra was evaluated in terms of sensitivity and specificity, with true positive (TP), false positive (FP), true negative (TN), and false negative (FN) results being key metrics. In Myanmar’s national survey and the subnational surveys in South Africa and Zambia, two Xpert Ultra tests were performed on separate sputum samples. This approach significantly improved sensitivity compared to a single test. The pooled sensitivity estimate for two tests on separate samples was 88% when trace results were considered positive. Comparatively, the sensitivity for a single test was 76%. When trace results were considered negative, the sensitivity was 64% for one test and 76% for two tests. Specificity was 97% when trace-positive results were counted as positive and 98% when they were counted as negative. The TREATS study highlighted that Xpert Ultra was more sensitive than solid culture methods, such as Ogawa, particularly in detecting tuberculosis (TB) cases that solid culture failed to identify. This finding underscores the limitations of solid culture methods, which are less sensitive than liquid culture (MGIT). The TREATS study also demonstrated that Xpert Ultra’s sensitivity was 87% (95% CI: 76–94%) when using two sputum samples, compared to 76% (95% CI: 64–86%) for a single sample. These results align with prior recommendations to test at least two separate sputum samples in prevalence surveys and routine clinical practice. The FIND study provided additional evidence comparing Xpert Ultra with solid culture (Löwenstein-Jensen, LJ) and liquid culture (MGIT). Xpert Ultra consistently outperformed LJ culture in sensitivity, both overall and across various subgroups, including smear-positive and smear-negative individuals. In smear-positive cases, nearly all individuals were Xpert-positive, but a proportion were solid-culture-negative. For smear-negative cases, Xpert Ultra demonstrated significantly higher sensitivity than solid culture. The FIND study also revealed challenges with solid culture testing in certain settings, such as Johannesburg, where all liquid-culture-positive samples were solid-culture-negative, indicating issues with solid culture performance. This highlights the variability in solid culture quality across different settings and the need for high-quality testing to ensure reliable results. Given these findings, the use of solid culture in future national TB prevalence surveys is no longer recommended as the initial diagnostic test. Instead, liquid culture should be prioritized as the microbiological reference standard for diagnosing pulmonary TB. If high-quality liquid culture testing is not feasible, Xpert Ultra offers a more sensitive and reproducible alternative. However, confirmatory testing with liquid culture is necessary for Xpert-positive results to address the risk of false positives. In summary, the evidence supports the adoption of diagnostic algorithms that incorporate Xpert Ultra testing, either alone or in combination with liquid culture, for future TB prevalence surveys. This approach ensures timely and accurate diagnosis while addressing the limitations of solid culture methods.
